title: cubic blog: Ultrareview | Launch week 03, Day 3
summary: Ultra-deep code reviews
body_text: 95% of PRs need fast, accurate feedback. The other 5% are complex, large or critical, and require the kind of deeper review you'd ask your CTO for. Our review agents rank #1 on Martian's Code Review benchmark : they're accurate and built for speed, with a cap on time and how many files can be reviewed per run. You get feedback in minutes, and that's the right tradeoff for most changes. But not for all of them. That's why we came up with ultrareview . An ultrareview is a deeper review mode that can take twice as much time, and three times as many tokens, giving our agents time and resources to research, trace, and find more complex bugs, while still catching every issue a regular review would find. They're the same reviews you already know, on steroids. We only use the best available models in the market for ultrareviews, and every Pro account gets 2 ultrareview runs included per seat per month. How to use After opening a PR, mention @cubic-dev-ai ultrareview in a new comment in the PR: This will trigger the new ultrareview and stop any regular review already running. Ultrareviews can take up to 45 minutes to run, even though they typically finish in under 30 minutes. How is this different from codebase scans? A codebase scan is a deep analysis of your entire codebase, running for 12+ hours. Ultrareviews sit in between standard PR reviews and codebase scans. They're deeper than a regular review, but less open-ended than a codebase scan (they're bound to the changes in your PR), with explicit execution limits (~45 minutes), and still fast enough to keep you shipping. Available today on the cubic Pro plan.

title: Moving from WordPress to Jekyll (and static site generators in general)
summary: Some technical notes on how and why we moved from WordPress to Jekyll, a well-known static site generator (SSG).
body_text: As I mentioned in my post earlier this week , we just completed a migration from WordPress to Jekyll . I outlined a couple of reasons for it but basically came down to preference, speed, and ability to make changes easily. Frameworks like Jekyll (or Astro ) aren’t for everybody, although they make a lot more sense in the general environment of AI proliferation, markdown becoming the lingua franca of LLMs, and a general trend toward headless sites. Everybody knows how insecure WordPress can be, although this is largely mitigated by working with a reputable host. The biggest issue was speed. As a platform company, we move very fast and we always felt limited by what we could do with WordPress and we were constantly bottlenecked by whether or not we had WP developers available. But it’s hard to find good developers for any framework and especially for WordPress. When you find someone who is good at WordPress development, it means they are good at pretty much everything else they try and so it feels like a waste of talent to have them work on WordPress. It’s like a built-in brain drain. Since the advent of coding agents like Claude Code , it has now become easier to completely route around this problem by simply migrating to another platform. We chose Jekyll for the reasons I’ll discuss in the next section. Architecture decisions that led to Jekyll Just last week, Cloudflare announced a new CMS framework that they have dubbed the “spiritual successor” to WordPress . It’s based on Astro, which is one of the most popular static site generators (SSG) right now. It looks great, but we wanted something that we had experience with and was a mature framework. As I mentioned in my previous post, our site ran on Jekyll long ago so we knew it well. For those who are not familiar: the biggest difference between a CMS like WordPress and an SSG is that there is no database (typically), nor even an application server in the latter. You’re working entirely in HTML templates, includes, layout files, config files, and then markdown for everything else. Metadata on the page is defined as frontmatter, which is the YAML data between the --- delimiters at the top of the markdown file. So, for example, the frontmatter for this post looks like this: layout : post title : " Moving from WordPress to Jekyll (and static site generators in general)" description : " Some technical notes on how and why we moved from WordPress to Jekyll, a well-known static site generator (SSG)." date : 2026-04-09 author : Ray Grieselhuber permalink : /blog/rebuilding-demandsphere-with-jekyll-and-claude-code/ tags : - Engineering - AI Search Other than that, these posts are just straight markdown. We start them in the _drafts folder and move them to the _posts folder when we’re ready to publish. Migrating 288 WordPress blog posts and other pages The area that took the most time, aside from the design, was properly migrating the existing content. The site itself has over 15 years of blog posts but, frankly, we didn’t need all of them. So, we used our GSC tools in DemandSphere to identify the pages that actually had valuable equity and used indexing data to make the call on which pages could be left unindexed - and simply deleted - as part of the migration. WordPress has an XML export that you can use to export everything, so we started with that. Fortunately, I was able to leverage Claude Code quite a bit to analyze each page in terms of the equity it had and very quickly filter out what we didn’t need. It took a little more fiddling to get featured images (and images in general) migrated over properly but this was also basically an export and an import. AI-assisted development with Claude Code Claude Code was basically what enabled us to do what we had wanted to do for years. Everyone on our team is so busy that we never would have had time to do a proper job of this migration. It didn’t make sense to hire out the work either. We heavily leveraged multiple sessions, CLAUDE.md, and a bunch of other .md files to keep the project on track. The dev tools we built The part where Claude Code really helped the most was in building nine separate dev tools that live right in the repository. We were able to leverage custom build scripts that keep these dev tools outside of the production build as well. The featured image of this post shows what the Dev Tools dashboard looks like. Most of these tools are managed by individual audit scripts dedicated to producing the output needed. So, for example, we have a lighthouse.js script, a site structure script, and so on. We built the following: Site Structure This was initially one of the most helpful tools, because it served as a tiny, onboard Screaming Frog type tool. We could easily spot URLs that weren’t on the sitemap, missing / duplicate metadata, etc. It also helped us spot URLs that belonged under different subfolders. Lighthouse Auditor As any SEO worth their salt will tell you, Lighthouse is about a lot more than just page speed and website performance. We made a lot of improvements and still have more to go. The fact that the site, in production, is all static obviously helps. Schema Auditor This is one that we will be doing more work on but it was a great tool to help us make sure we had a baseline of schema data in place. AEO Auditor The AEO auditor tool is far from comprehensive but helped us cover a lot of the basics. Schema Details The Schema Details tool helped us to analyze, page by page, what we needed to improve in terms of coverage. Open Graph Preview The Open Graph preview tool I use a lot, because this one lets us preview how a page will look when shared on socials. Within the tool, you can click on each page and it will pop up a viewer that shows how it will look in Facebook, LinkedIn, X, and Slack. I can see that I already have a page to fix after finishing this post. Content Similarity - Topic Clusters After the migration was complete, I added this one because I wanted to get an understanding of the semantic clustering of the site. We vectorized the entire site using the all-MiniLM-L6-v2 model, a nice, 384-dimensional embeddings model that runs completely locally, from @xenova/transformers . It was more than sufficient for this first run. Content Similarity - Topic Table The embeddings also enabled the creation of a few more subtools. First up was a topic table. This one still needs some more work and adjustment of the parameters but it gave us a decent overview of the major topics covered. Content Similarity - Similar Pairs We also generated a content similarity report, so we can go back and either combine / merge content that is overly similar or spend time on each one to make it more differentiated, if that makes sense to do. Content Similarity - Semantic Cores The semantic core concept is one of the key things to understand about any site, in my opinion, because it’s related to how the LLMs and search engines understand, at a general level, what your site is about. Internal Linking Internal link auditing, when you have the embeddings of a site, is one of the best processes you can run in order to help the engines understand which topics and pages are most related. I never liked the tools that were available for WordPress for this, so we’re happy to have this now. We do have a lot of optimization to do here, however. Redirects The Redirects tool was invaluable in making sure that we didn’t miss anything important. As we can easily see in each one of these, our job is far from over in putting the finishing touches on the site but we’re in a much better place to fix remaining issues and know exactly what to focus on. Client-side search with no external dependencies Jekyll generates a /search.json file at build time. It’s a JSON array of every page and post with title, URL, content (up to 400 characters), tags, date, and type indexed in the file. The search page fetches a single JSON file, runs substring matching in the browser. It scores each element of the metadata (e.g., title 10x, tags 5x, etc) with weights, and caps the results returned at 30. This allowed us to have full site indexing and search capability with no Algolia , no Elastic, no Lunr.js, no server API. The current stats are 398 entries and this will easily scale to 2,500-3,000 pages before we need to make any optimizations. We estimate that search latency will still stay sub-3ms even at 5,000 pages, so we’re good for a long time. SEO architecture We wanted structured data on every page from day one. Every page on the site has JSON-LD schema - Organization and WebSite on all pages, BreadcrumbList on everything except the homepage, FAQPage on any page with FAQ content, BlogPosting on blog posts, and SoftwareApplication on product pages. The FAQ schema is generated automatically from front matter. We add a faq_schema block to the YAML and the template handles the rest. No manual JSON-LD editing is necessary. This is how we got to 470+ FAQ entries across 128 pages without spending too much time. Canonical tags, Open Graph meta, and the RSS feed all use site.url so they resolve correctly per environment. The robots.txt is environment-aware too - staging blocks all bots except Screaming Frog and Sitebulb , production allows everything. GTM and Google Analytics only load after the user accepts the cookie consent banner. On staging, the consent banner doesn’t even render. This keeps our analytics clean and our staging environment invisible to tracking. The sitemap is handled by the jekyll-sitemap plugin, which just generates it from the build output. No manual maintenance. One thing I didn’t expect to spend time on was Content Security Policy headers. Every time we deployed, something new would break: first Cloudflare’s own analytics beacon was blocked, then Google Ads conversion tracking, then the Leaflet map library on our international SEO page. We went through about six rounds of CSP updates before everything was clean. Production cutover We run two environments on Cloudflare Pages from the same repo. The main branch is production, and any other branch deploys as a preview. The build.sh script checks the CF_PAGES_BRANCH environment variable and sets JEKYLL_ENV accordingly. Production builds remove the dev-tools directory and keep the sitemap. Staging builds remove the sitemap and add noindex headers. The DNS cutover was straightforward because we already managed our DNS in Cloudflare. Adding www.demandsphere.com as a custom domain on the Pages project automatically swapped the CNAME from Kinsta to Pages. After the cutover, we ran a Screaming Frog crawl and found a few issues to fix. We also found that our favicon wasn’t showing up in Google’s search results. Two problems: the root /favicon.ico was returning a 404 because we hadn’t copied it to the root directory, and our PNG favicon was only 32x32 pixels. Google requires at least 48x48. We added a 96x96 PNG, a 48x48 PNG, a web manifest, and a proper multi-size ICO at the root. Google’s favicon cache is slow to update, but the technical setup is now correct. What’s next There’s still a lot to do. We have about 65 images over 100KB that need optimization. Most of our 288 migrated blog posts only have a generic “Blog” tag and could use proper categorization. It’s working well overall, and we’re very happy with the migration. We can now execute on new content ideas far faster and at much higher quality than we have ever been able to do so before.

title: Retirement Realities

body_text: Retirement Realities Highlights Many workers 60+ expect never to fully retire—and most say money is the reason Over 4 in 10 workers 60+ say they'll never fully stop working—and 60% say it's because they can't afford to. The typical 60+ American has saved $100K toward a $250K goal, leaving them $150K short at the start of retirement. Social Security is doing most of the heavy lifting in retirement Nearly half (47%) of adults 60+ rely on Social Security as their primary income source. Among the fully retired, that rises to 71%. Inflation, healthcare, and caregiving are reshaping retirement Inflation is the #1 retirement worry (62%), ahead of healthcare (59%) and outliving savings (42%). 30% of still-working adults 60+ stay employed to keep healthcare coverage. Another 42% stay employed to cover caregiving costs. Phased retirement could help employers keep older workers longer 61% of workers 60+ would stay in the workforce longer if offered a phased retirement arrangement. Over 4 in 10 workers 60+ say they will never fully stop working—and 60% say it's because they can't afford to Working later in life is not always a lifestyle choice. Longer life expectancy may be pushing some milestones later, but for many older adults, work in later life is driven by financial pressure. By the numbers: 42% of still-working adults 60+ say they'll never fully stop working for pay. 60% of those say financial necessity is keeping them from retiring. 61% of still-working adults 60+ are delaying retirement past their original target date. $100K median retirement savings vs. $250K stated goal. 63% say their savings are inadequate. 47% rely on Social Security as their primary income source. But for many older workers, staying in the workforce also means facing age discrimination that creates barriers to their goals and progress. 22% of those 60+ have experienced ageism in their careers. 56% of those say hiring barriers are the main way it shows up. Retirement confidence is split: nearly half of fully retired workers 60+ say their savings fall short For the 60+ population that does make it to retirement, the reality is not always all it’s chalked up to be. Only 49% of fully retired adults say their savings are sufficient. 42% of fully retired adults say savings fall short, and they need to change their lifestyle plans. The large gap between the median savings of $100k and the mean savings of over $639K shows how uneven retirement preparedness is, as most retirement wealth is concentrated at the top. A small group is well-prepared, but most older adults are not. That gap is changing what retirement looks like for people without enough savings. Those who have yet to retire are more likely to extend their work life (58%, vs 38% overall) to close the savings gap; those already retired are figuring out how to make do with what they have (42% vs 25% overall). Women face a retirement savings crisis Older women, who faced significant barriers to earning equal pay compared to men throughout their careers, bear a disproportionate burden of the savings gap. Women 60+ have a median of $60,000 saved Men 60+ have a median of $199,000 saved That's a $139,000 gender gap in median retirement savings Unmarried women 60+ have an even larger gap, with a median savings of only $19,500 . 28% of women 60+have zero savings , a significantly larger share than the 16% of 60+ men. “ You don’t need to be a financial expert to start saving smartly. Invest your retirement savings in index funds to maximize growth. Look for companies that offer 401K matching and immediate vesting. ” — Sam DeMase, ZipRecruiter Career Expert The gender wage gap grows over the course of a career , and many older women find themselves at a loss when they approach retirement. Starting to save early in a career, focusing on fields with better gender pay ratios , and negotiating during the offer phase are all ways women in the workforce can now prepare themselves for a successful retirement. The savings gap between the goal and reality will worsen without intervention Being financially unprepared, or seeing costs rise faster than their semi-fixed income can support, is pushing many retirees back to the workforce. Semi-retired workers have a median of $80K saved , down from the $100K that fully retired workers have. The gap is part of the reason semi-retirees haven’t fully let go. Unretired workers have a median of just $50K saved . Running low on savings is driving these prior retirees back to work. For younger workers, understanding the goal and how to prepare for it early can be make or break for their retirement strategies. Many young workers are facing growing challenges —carrying student debt, facing high housing costs and inflation, and a variable labor market—all things that can disrupt a fragile retirement plan. The good news: younger workers are starting to save earlier, especially with automatic 401(k) enrollment . Given the reliance on Social Security for today’s retirees’ income and the uncertain future of the vital government program, saving more today will be critical. Advice for Gen Z and Millennials Start saving now, a 10-year delay creates a wealth gap that's difficult to close. Seek employer 401(k) matching of 6%+ and negotiate for the highest match possible; contribute the maximum per paycheck. Look for "immediate vesting" rather than a 3-5 year waiting period. Ask if your employer matches student loan payments with retirement contributions—many now do. “ Take advantage of compound interest and start saving and investing now. Give your future self flexibility to take a career break or a lower-paying job you love. ” — Sam DeMase, ZipRecruiter Career Expert 71% of fully retired workers rely on Social Security as their primary income source — vs. just 4.3% who cite 401(k) distributions The concentration of retirement income in a single government program represents a systemic vulnerability across the 60+ population, especially for fully-retired workers. Inflation is changing retirement plans 20% say inflation has directly delayed their retirement timeline. 20% have changed their planned retirement lifestyle because of it. 8% say inflation will cause them to return to work after retirement. 62% name inflation as their #1 retirement worry — above healthcare (59%) and outliving savings (42%). Healthcare is keeping people at work 30% of still-working adults 60+ stay employed to keep healthcare coverage. Retirement isn't financially viable for many without a coverage plan. Caregiving is delaying retirement 42% of still-working adults 60+ stay employed specifically to cover caregiving costs or to maintain healthcare for those they care for. 36% of semi-retired workers returned to work for the same reason. 24% of the 60+ population is currently providing caregiving or financial support to a family member; the largest group is caring for adult children (12%). Layoffs derailed retirement timelines 25% of those 60+ experienced a layoff at some point in their career. Of those, 32% say it delayed retirement by at least a year due to lost income, savings, and benefits. For semi-retired workers, returning to work isn't always about money While the financial benefits of work are essential to many older workers, other considerations, such as maintaining a routine and finding purpose in their work, are keeping this population engaged in their careers. 41% of semi-retired workers returned to work to stay productive and busy. 39% work because they derive purpose and meaning from their jobs. 26% went back for social connection. That comes as nearly 3 in 10 semi-retired workers work remotely . Flexible work options can help older workers stay engaged in the workplace longer. Work offers more than just financial compensation; when employers offer work that provides flexibility, purpose, and connection, they can better meet the needs of older workers while retaining experienced talent. 61% of workers 60+ would stay in the workforce longer if offered a phased arrangement A gradual wind-down through reduced hours, consulting, or mentorship could help workers ease into retirement while helping employers avoid losing decades of institutional knowledge at once. 38% of those 60+ still-working say they would stay five or more additional years under a phased arrangement. This would keep a key segment of the workforce engaged, softening the impact of the impending retirement cliff. Only 39% of all 60+ say they would not stay longer, regardless of the arrangement offered. Planning for a gradual wind-down, instead of a sudden stop, may become the new normal. Methodology This survey was administered to a nationally representative sample of 1,500 US residents aged 60+ who have ever worked. The survey was fielded between February 11 and March 7, 2026, by Pure Spectrum. The sample included a mix of those who are fully retired, not retired, and semi-retired/unretired.

title: Pathward Names Maren Hock 2025 Volunteer of the Year
summary: Pathward names Maren Hock as its 2025 Volunteer of the Year, recognizing her leadership, community service, and $5,000 donation to Harmony South Dakota.
body_text: April 20, 2026 – Pathward’s Volunteer of the Year award recognizes an employee for their unwavering commitment to the betterment of their community through volunteerism. Each year, the employee is selected through a peer nomination process and invited to direct a $5,000 company donation to their qualifying nonprofit of choice. As we celebrate Volunteer Week, Pathward is pleased to recognize Maren Hock, Manager of Shared Services Operations, as our 2025 Volunteer of the Year! Since childhood, Hock has understood that giving back doesn’t need to be financial to be meaningful. Over the years, driven by the support she and her family received during challenging seasons, Hock’s work has connected her to a range of causes, from food insecurity to housing and education, and support for veterans and their families. Her commitment to these issues has led to years of sustained service across several Sioux Falls-based and regional organizations. From hands-on volunteering to board service, event coordination, and skills-based support, Hock truly embodies the spirit of service at the heart of Pathward. What’s more, she leads Pathward’s Military Veterans Network Employee Resource Group and champions volunteerism, frequently organizing events and encouraging her colleagues to get involved. As part of her recognition, Hock has directed a $5,000 company donation to Harmony South Dakota . Hock shared, “Nonprofits have truly changed my life. I’m so thankful for these organizations because they’ve not only helped me develop, but they’ve also helped me develop my children. Just knowing firsthand the impact that these organizations can have and how they can shape and change the trajectory of people’s lives has been heartening. “Volunteering has given me a deep appreciation for access, dignity, and opportunity. Pathward as an organization aims to reach those who are underserved by traditional banking – and that intention bleeds into everything we do by centering people and being intentional. I see volunteerism as an extension of my role because I’m so proud to work for a company that values community and encourages us to show up in everything that we do outside of work.” Through Pathward’s Community Impact Program, eligible employees can take 16 hours of Volunteer Time Off each year. Also, by logging volunteer hours, employees can direct up to $480 per year to their favorite qualifying nonprofit through our Dollars for Doers program. Learn more about how Pathward is giving back in our 2025 Impact Report . Pathward encourages employee engagement in the communities we serve, and Hock exemplifies this. title: The 2026 Academic Conference Playbook: How to Organize an Academic Conference from Call for Papers to Poster Sessions
summary: Planning an academic conference in 2026? This step-by-step playbook covers how to organize an academic conference from call for papers to poster sessions. Le...
body_text: Introduction Academic conferences are the lifeblood of scholarly exchange, but how to organize an academic conference successfully is a complex endeavour. From issuing a call for papers to orchestrating poster sessions on-site, organizers must juggle academic and logistical challenges. In 2026, conference planning takes on new dimensions – hybrid formats are common, global attendance is rebounding, and expectations for seamless execution are higher than ever. This guide serves as a comprehensive academic conference planning guide, walking through each step in detail. Whether you’re a first-time faculty chair or a seasoned planner, these proven strategies (backed by real examples and hard-won lessons) will help you create an impactful, collaborative event. Today’s conference environment is dynamic: in 2023, the global conference industry hosted 36.5 million in-person attendees, representing an 82% rebound in global conference attendance from 2021 . The average conference now attracts around 2,345 attendees , and academic gatherings are a key part of this surge. Some scholarly meetings remain intimate 100-person symposia, while others are massive international congresses – for instance, the American Geophysical Union’s Fall Meeting convenes over 25,000 attendees from more than 100 countries . Regardless of scale, the fundamental steps to plan an academic conference are similar, involving careful coordination of content, people, and infrastructure. In the sections that follow, we break down these steps to plan an academic conference, from the initial call for papers through to the closing poster session. How to Organize an Academic Conference: Planning Foundations Setting Objectives, Budget, and Team Every successful conference starts with a strong foundation. The organizing committee should first define the conference’s objectives and scope . Is the goal to share cutting-edge research in a niche field, foster interdisciplinary collaboration, or perhaps kickstart a new scholarly community? Clarifying the mission will guide all decisions, from session topics to target audience. Experienced organizers know that academic conference planning works best when objectives are specific and measurable – for example, aiming for 200 paper submissions, 500 attendees, and representation from 30 countries. Clear goals also help determine key success metrics. Academic events often measure ROI not in profit but in knowledge exchange: think post-conference survey scores, number of new collaborations sparked, or citations of presented papers . Next, form your organizing team . This typically includes a Conference Chair or Co-chairs (often senior faculty) to provide academic leadership, plus leads for key areas: a Program Chair to oversee the scholarly content (papers, peer review, scheduling), a Logistics/Operations Lead for venue and vendor management, a Sponsorship/Finance Lead for budget and fundraising, and a Marketing/Communications Lead to handle promotions and delegate outreach. Many academic conferences bring together faculty and professional planners – blending subject-matter expertise with event management know-how. If you’re working with a professional conference organizer or PCO, clarify the division of roles early. Also consider student volunteers or a local committee if the event is hosted on a campus; they can assist with on-site tasks and bring enthusiasm to the team. Building Your Academic Dream Team — How a balanced leadership team ensures academic and logistical success Establish a realistic budget at the outset. Even non-profit academic conferences require detailed budgeting for venue costs, catering, printing, A/V equipment, and social events. Estimate revenue from registration fees, institutional support, and sponsors (like academic publishers or industry partners) and ensure expenses don’t exceed income. Seasoned planners advise building a 10% contingency for surprises – there are always last-minute costs. If your conference is recurring annually or biennially, leverage historical data to inform your budget. For instance, analyzing last year’s costs versus attendance can reveal trends in catering needs or swag orders by leveraging historical data and benchmarks for profitable events . Academic associations often have guidelines for typical budget allocations (e.g., 40% venue and catering, 20% A/V, 15% social events, etc.), which provide a helpful starting point. And remember, sound budgeting isn’t just about cutting costs – it’s about ensuring the conference delivers value in line with its expenditures. Tip: If cash flow is a challenge (say, you must pay venue deposits well before registration income comes in), explore creative financing options. University departments or grant agencies might advance funds. Additionally, modern event platforms offer support like upfront funding programs – for example, Ticket Fairy’s event capital program can provide an advance against future ticket sales to cover early expenses. Use such solutions judiciously, but know they exist to help organisers bridge funding gaps. Ready to Sell Tickets? Create professional event pages with built-in payment processing, marketing tools, and real-time analytics. Create Your Event Event Ticketing Software Timeline and Key Milestones Academic conferences involve many moving parts, so working from a master timeline is essential. Start planning 12–18 months in advance for large international conferences, and at least 6–9 months for smaller events. Below is a rough timeline outlining steps in organizing a successful academic conference: Timeline (Months Before) Key Planning Milestones 12+ months Define conference goals and theme. Form the organizing committee and roles. Draft a preliminary budget. Evaluate and secure a venue or host location (university, hotel, convention center). Set the event dates (avoiding major holidays and competing conferences). 9–12 months Announce the Call for Papers (CFP) and submission guidelines. Launch the conference website with key information. Begin outreach to attract paper submissions and delegates. If inviting high-profile keynote speakers, start contacting them now (top professors’ calendars fill quickly!). Finalize venue booking and any required permits or contracts . 6–9 months Close the call for papers and start the peer review process for submitted abstracts/papers. Secure sponsorships and define sponsor packages (exhibitor booths, logo placements, sponsored sessions). Open early-bird registration for attendees (offer discounted rates to drive early sign-ups). Plan the framework of the conference programme (number of days, parallel tracks, social events). 3–6 months Announce accepted papers and notify authors (include clear instructions for preparing presentations or camera-ready papers). Publish a preliminary agenda or at least the list of sessions/tracks to entice attendees. Continue marketing the conference via academic networks, mailing lists, and social media. Arrange accommodations partnerships – e.g., negotiate hotel room blocks for out-of-town attendees as part of your pre-conference networking and engagement strategy . Finalize any travel grants or special initiatives (such as student travel awards or diversity scholarships). 1–3 months Finalize the detailed conference schedule (assign dates/times for each session, poster slot, keynote, etc.). Coordinate with the venue on room layouts, A/V setups, catering menus, and Wi-Fi arrangements. Order or print materials: badges, lanyards, signage, banners, programme booklets (or set up a conference app). Arrange shipments of any equipment or exhibit materials. Recruit and train volunteers or brief the event staff on their roles. Test-run virtual platforms or registration equipment as needed. Weeks prior Send reminders to registrants with practical info (venue maps, COVID or safety protocols, what to bring). For presenters, collect final papers or slides if required and ensure all A/V content is loaded. Double-check all technology – registration systems, projectors, microphones, live-stream feeds – to avoid day-of glitches. Create a contingency plan for common issues (speaker no-show, power outage, etc.). Experienced organizers often have a “conference day kit” ready with spare laptop adapters, clickers, and printed agendas for on-site use. Conference days Execute flawlessly: conduct morning briefings with your team, ensure registration check-in is smooth and quick, keep sessions on schedule, and facilitate speaker needs. Promote engagement by encouraging Q&A and networking. Be ready to troubleshoot in real-time – from resolving A/V issues to rearranging sessions if a presenter is missing. Stay flexible and maintain communication (two-way radios or a staff WhatsApp group can be invaluable for instant updates). Most importantly, take time to observe attendee experience : Is the signage clear? Are people networking? Use this insight to make on-the-fly improvements (e.g., adjusting room temperatures, adding extra chairs to a packed session). Post-conference The work isn’t over! Send a thank-you email to attendees and presenters. Collect feedback via online surveys – what worked and what didn’t? Share conference outcomes: publish proceedings or session recordings, and consider writing an event summary for your website or association newsletter. If sponsors were involved, provide them a post-event report with metrics (number of leads from their booth, visibility impressions, attendee demographics). Finally, debrief within the organizing team to document lessons learned for next time. This timeline can be adjusted to your event’s needs, but it underscores a key point: planning a conference is a marathon, not a sprint. By pacing tasks over months, you reduce last-minute chaos and ensure each aspect – from abstract submissions to catering orders – gets the attention it deserves. Utilize project management tools or simple shared spreadsheets to track progress. Many veteran organisers also hold bi-weekly planning calls with their committee to keep everyone aligned. As you progress through the timeline, you’ll move from broad planning into the finer details, which we’ll explore in the next sections. Balancing Your Conference Budget — Why strategic fund allocation protects your event from financial surprises Launching the Call for Papers and Managing Submissions Crafting and Promoting the Call for Papers For academic conferences, the Call for Papers (CFP) is where it all begins. This announcement is your rallying cry to the research community, so make it clear, compelling, and broadly visible. A strong CFP typically includes the conference theme or topics of interest, the types of submissions accepted (e.g., full papers, extended abstracts, posters), key dates (submission deadline, notification date, early registration deadlines), and submission guidelines (formatting requirements, word/page limits, and how to submit). Emphasize what makes your conference attractive – will there be renowned keynote professors? Publication opportunities in a journal or proceedings? Unique workshop sessions or awards for best paper? Highlight these to motivate researchers to submit their work. Dissemination of the call for papers is critical. In 2026, digital channels have the widest reach: create a dedicated webpage for the CFP and share it via university departments, academic mailing lists, professional societies, and social media. Many fields have popular listservs or forums (such as ACM SIG mailing lists in computer science or discipline-specific Slack groups) where CFPs can be posted – leverage those networks. Don’t underestimate the power of personal outreach either: committee members should share the CFP with colleagues and at related events. If your budget allows, advertise the conference on scholarly platforms like ResearchGate or professional hubs. The goal is to cast a wide net so that you attract a diverse, high-quality pool of submissions. Organizers of major conferences often announce the CFP at least a year in advance at prior events (for example, presenting a slide about next year’s conference dates and CFP details at the closing of this year’s conference). Starting early gives researchers time to plan studies and papers to submit. Free Tool: Will the Room Actually Be Full? Forecasts expected attendance from ticket type, event type and day of week. Calculates safe over-book count for free-RSVP events. Free estimator. No-Show Rate Estimator See All Free Tools When promoting the CFP, ensure there’s a smooth funnel from interest to action. Provide a direct link to submit abstracts online via a user-friendly platform. Rather than using email submissions (which can become chaotic), most conferences use abstract management software or an online submission form. Depending on your budget and needs, you might choose a free platform like EasyChair for a smaller academic conference or a more robust conference management system (ConfTool, Ex Ordo, Oxford Abstracts, etc.) for larger events – some systems handle everything from submissions to the programme schedule. The chosen system should support your review process (e.g., double-blind review if you require anonymized submissions) and scale to the expected volume. Keep in mind that some all-in-one conference ticketing software can integrate registration with submission data, but often you’ll manage paper submissions in a dedicated system and use a separate platform for attendee registration and ticketing. Finally, set your submission deadline strategically. Give at least 8–12 weeks from the CFP announcement to the deadline so researchers have time to prepare quality submissions. It’s common to see a deadline extension of a week or two – many academic conference planning guides suggest building this into your timeline, since a brief extension can significantly boost submission numbers (procrastination is real in academia!). If you do extend, announce it quickly and widely. Pro tip: avoid deadline dates that clash with major holidays or other big conferences in your field. And clearly communicate the deadline timezone (e.g., “11:59 PM Pacific Time”) to avoid confusion for international authors. Navigating Your Planning Timeline — How a structured 18-month roadmap keeps complex projects on track Peer Review and Selection Process Once the submissions roll in – possibly hundreds or even thousands – the next challenge is managing the peer review process. Academic conferences live or die by the quality of their content, so a rigorous and fair review is essential for maintaining credibility. Start by assembling a Program Committee (PC) of knowledgeable reviewers, usually professors or industry researchers in relevant subfields. Assign a Program Chair or a few Track Chairs to coordinate reviewers and make final decisions in each topic area. Each submitted paper or abstract should be reviewed by multiple experts (typically 2–4 reviewers per submission). To ensure fairness and avoid bias, adopt the appropriate review model: many conferences use double-blind review , where reviewers do not see author names and vice versa. Make sure your submission system supports this (e.g., by allowing authors to upload a “blind” version of their paper without identifying information). Distribute the workload evenly among reviewers based on expertise. It’s helpful to let reviewers bid on or indicate which papers match their expertise, then use the system’s algorithm or manual assignment to allocate submissions. Set a reasonable review period (4–6 weeks is standard for an academic conference) and provide clear review guidelines. For instance, outline the criteria such as originality, methodology, significance, and clarity. Encourage constructive feedback – even rejected papers should ideally get useful comments to help authors improve. Stay in communication with your reviewers; send reminders as deadlines approach, and be prepared to recruit a few emergency reviewers if someone drops out. In large conferences, it’s common for organizers to have to chase last-minute reviews to ensure every paper gets the required number of evaluations. After reviews are in, the Program Committee must select the final presentations . Use a combination of quantitative scores and qualitative discussion. Often, PC meetings (virtual or in-person) are held to debate borderline cases or to ensure diversity of topics. Aim for a program that reflects the breadth of the field and the goals you set. Some conferences accept a high percentage of submissions to be inclusive and maximise knowledge sharing, while others are highly selective to showcase only top-tier research. For example, NeurIPS 2022 – a premier AI conference – received over 10,400 paper submissions and accepted only about 2,672 papers for a 25.7% acceptance rate , reflecting its competitive nature. On the other hand, a small regional symposium might accept 80% of submissions if they meet basic quality standards, focusing more on community building. Align your acceptance rate with the conference’s ethos and logistical capacity (number of presentation slots available). Launching Your Call For Papers — How a clear submission funnel attracts high-quality global research When decisions are ready, send out notification emails to authors. Congratulate those accepted and provide next steps (registration details, presentation guidelines, deadlines for submitting final papers or slides). For declined papers, have a polite, encouraging tone and include reviewer feedback if possible – this reinforces the conference’s reputability and helps authors learn. Be prepared for some authors to withdraw even after acceptance (common reasons are inability to travel, visa issues, or their research not being ready). To mitigate empty slots in the program, you might accept a handful more papers than you have room for, or maintain a short waitlist of papers that could be promoted if space opens. Tracking author registrations can also signal potential drop-outs; if an accepted author hasn’t registered by the presenter deadline, send a reminder and gently inquire if they still plan to attend. Analytics in your submission system can flag discrepancies (e.g., two reviewers wildly diverging in scores on the same paper). As a chair, you might solicit an extra review in such cases or discuss in the committee to reach a resolution. And always keep an eye on ethical issues – if a paper raises plagiarism or sensitive content flags, have a process ready to investigate and handle it discreetly. By the end of this phase, you should have a confirmed roster of papers, posters, and perhaps panel proposals that will form the backbone of your conference programme. Designing the Conference Programme and Scholarly Tracks Building the Agenda: Tracks, Sessions, and Formats With the content selected, it’s time to design an engaging conference programme . Academic conferences often span multiple days and parallel streams, so careful planning is needed to maximize impact without overwhelming attendees. Start by grouping accepted presentations into thematic sessions or tracks . Review the topics of the papers – natural groupings will emerge (for example, in a biology conference you might have sessions on Genomics, Ecology, Biochemistry, etc.). Assign each session a descriptive title to attract audience interest. If your conference covers a broad discipline, consider designated tracks with their own sequence of sessions (e.g., Track A: “AI Algorithms”, Track B: “AI in Healthcare”, etc.). Appointing Session Chairs (often one of the reviewers or a senior author from that session) to moderate each session is a best practice; they can keep time and facilitate audience questions, ensuring professional execution. Mastering Double-Blind Peer Review — Why rigorous anonymized evaluation maintains your conference's scholarly integrity Next, map out the schedule grid . Many events follow a rhythm: start the day with a high-profile keynote or plenary when everyone is fresh, then break into parallel sessions, with coffee breaks and lunch providing natural pauses. Avoid scheduling too many popular sessions against each other – if two talks target the same sub-audience, try placing them sequentially instead of concurrently. It’s also wise to leave short buffers (5–10 minutes) between sessions for room transitions. Tools like spreadsheets or specialised scheduling software can help visualize this; some conference platforms allow drag-and-drop scheduling where you can see potential conflicts. Keep in mind any specific constraints: for instance, if a presenter has two papers, ensure their talks are in different sessions (and ideally not back-to-back if they’re in separate rooms). A well-structured agenda will let attendees easily navigate without feeling they’ve missed “the only session on X topic” due to a conflict. In designing your programme, diversify session formats to enhance engagement. Research talks (lecture-style presentations of papers) will be the staple, but consider adding panels, workshops, roundtables, or interactive forums for variety. Many 2026 conferences are moving beyond the classic format to keep audiences energized. For example, some academic events incorporate “ lightning talk ” sessions where presenters get 5 minutes each, or poster blitzes where poster authors each share a one-slide summary to the whole group, enticing people to visit their poster. According to veteran meeting professionals, variety is key: blending traditional talks with Q&As, small-group discussions, and hands-on activities caters to different learning styles and prevents conference fatigue. One conference programming playbook suggests balancing marquee keynotes with plenty of networking-friendly sessions for maximum impact. Ultimately, a mix of formats can elevate the attendee experience from passive listening to active participation. For clarity, here’s a summary of common academic conference session formats and their roles: Mixing Dynamic Session Formats — Why varied presentation styles keep audiences energized and engaged Session Format Typical Duration Purpose and Characteristics Example Use Case Keynote Talk 30–60 minutes Plenary session featuring a distinguished speaker for big-picture insights. Often open to all attendees without parallel sessions. A Nobel laureate or renowned professor shares visionary perspectives in the opening session. Paper Presentations (Oral Session) 15–20 minutes per talk (plus Q&A) Standard research talks grouped into themed sessions. Speakers present their study and answer questions. Multiple sessions may run in parallel. Five AI researchers each present their latest findings in a 90-minute “Machine Learning Algorithms” session. Panel Discussion 45–60 minutes A moderated discussion among 3–5 experts on a specific topic, followed by audience Q&A. Offers multiple viewpoints and debate. A panel of climate scientists and policy makers discusses “Future of Renewable Energy” with questions from the audience. Workshop/Tutorial 2–3 hours (often pre- or post-conference) In-depth, interactive session focused on skill-building or deep dives into a subject. May involve practical exercises or training components. An optional pre-conference workshop teaches attendees a new statistical analysis method through hands-on exercises. Poster Session 1–2 hours (open flow) Dozens of researchers simultaneously present posters (large research posters on display). Attendees walk around, chat one-on-one with authors. Informal and highly interactive. An evening poster reception with 100 posters on display; attendees grab a refreshment and network while discussing poster findings. Networking Event 1–2 hours Social or unstructured time designed for attendees to mingle, build connections, and discuss collaborations in a relaxed setting. A conference dinner or welcome reception at a local museum where attendees socialize and meet peers from other institutions. Design your agenda to incorporate these elements in a logical flow. For example, Day 1 might begin with a keynote, then move through paper sessions, and end with a poster reception and welcome banquet. Day 2 could include a morning panel discussion bridging multiple disciplines, and perhaps a free evening for attendees to explore the city or join self-organized meetups. If you have more content than fits in oral sessions, utilize poster sessions liberally – they are efficient for showcasing a large number of projects and encourage direct interaction. Collect Any Attendee Data at Checkout Add custom registration fields to your checkout — dietary needs, t-shirt sizes, company names, and more. Conditional logic and per-ticket-type fields. Custom Event Registration Fields Get Started Free Throughout program design, maintain flexibility . Inevitably, you’ll face last-minute changes: a speaker might cancel due to an emergency, or perhaps you’ll get attendee feedback that two sessions should swap times for better flow. Prepare a Plan B for key sessions. Many experienced organisers keep one slot open for a “backup talk” or have a respected attendee ready to give an impromptu seminar if needed. In one case, a major physics conference had a keynote presenter stuck overseas due to a flight cancellation – the organisers quickly moved an afternoon plenary speaker up to the morning slot and filled the afternoon with an expert panel on hot topics in physics, salvaging the day. The lesson is adaptability : design your schedule robustly enough to handle the unexpected. Using a digital agenda (via a conference app or website) can also ease last-minute adjustments, as changes can be pushed out to attendees instantly, avoiding outdated printed schedules. Integrating Keynote Professors and Invited Speakers A highlight of many academic conferences is the keynote or plenary speakers – often luminaries in the field whose talks draw large audiences and can set the tone for the event. Securing a great keynote requires early planning and careful courting. Identify a short-list of ideal speakers (celebrated researchers, influential thought leaders, or even industry pioneers relevant to your theme). Reach out as early as possible – top professors’ calendars fill up fast, sometimes over a year in advance. When extending an invitation, personalize it: explain why their contribution would be valued and how it aligns with the conference’s goals. If applicable, mention if you can offer an honorarium, travel reimbursement, or special recognition (academics are often motivated by the opportunity to influence their field and to network, but a reasonable honorarium and covering expenses is a courtesy). For many academic events, keynote speakers may not charge the hefty fees seen in corporate conferences; instead, they might be satisfied with travel coverage and the prestige of the platform. If a session is overflowing with attendees standing in back, consider a quick intervention like opening partition walls (if possible) or encouraging them to find seating on the floor in front (some prefer that to standing). Always have a Plan B: if a room is too packed, know which is your backup space or be ready to repeat a popular session later in a larger hall. On a related note, use your announcements or apps to communicate real-time advisories (“Workshop X is filling up fast; additional seating is available in overflow Room Y with a video feed”). This is similar to crowd management strategies used in large-scale conventions , adapted to academic settings. Optimizing Your Venue Layout — Why logical room clustering and accessibility enhance the attendee journey Time management is one area academic meetings traditionally struggle with – sessions running over can cascade into chaos. Emphasize a strict schedule: instruct session chairs to stick to time and politely cut off long-winded speakers or Q&As if needed. Having a centrally controlled clock or timer can help. Also, build in a few minutes between sessions in the agenda for reset. If things do get behind by midday, lunchtime is often when you can “reset” by slightly shortening the break (announce it clearly if you do) to catch up. Attendees generally appreciate punctuality; it allows them to move between tracks and not miss talks. Handling Challenges and Crisis Scenarios No matter how much you plan, reality will throw curveballs. Effective on-site management means anticipating these and reacting calmly under pressure. Let’s examine some common issues and how to handle them like a pro: Speaker No-Show or Delay: Despite confirmations, a speaker might miss their session (travel delays, illness, etc.). If a presenter is simply running late, you might resequence talks (e.g., take the next talk first) or extend Q&A of the previous speaker to fill time. If a speaker is a no-show entirely, do not just leave an empty slot – attendees will drift away and it reduces the session’s value. Options include having the session chair prepare a few slides to spark a discussion with the audience on the topic, or if another presenter in the room has extra material, invite them to share more. Some conferences have a couple of “backup” talks from local researchers who can step in on short notice if needed. Communicate any changes to the audience transparently: e.g., “Unfortunately, Dr. X couldn’t be here. We’ll use this time for an open discussion on the session theme.” Often, attendees appreciate the chance for an unstructured discussion, which can be quite engaging. Technical Failures: Projector bulbs fry, mics produce feedback, video live streams drop – tech issues are inevitable. The key is rapid response and managing attendee expectations. Ensure that at least one technician or knowledgeable staff is monitoring each keynote and major session actively. If a critical system fails (say, the main hall projector dies mid-keynote), have an immediate backup plan: perhaps the speaker can continue with a verbal talk if slides aren’t vital, or switch to a spare projector if available. Communicate clearly: a quick announcement like “Please bear with us, we’re resolving a technical issue” helps maintain patience. In one memorable incident, a keynote’s slideshow wouldn’t advance due to a laptop crash – the organizer had the presence of mind to invite the audience to gather around closer while the speaker delivered a more informal talk sans slides, turning a tech failure into an intimate fireside chat moment. People still rated the session highly because of the authenticity and quick thinking displayed. Managing Unexpected Event Challenges — How proactive contingency planning saves the day when issues arise Venue or Environmental Issues: External problems like power outages, fire alarms, or even sudden weather events can disrupt things. Know the venue’s emergency procedures and have them handy. If a fire alarm rings, even if false, calmly direct attendees to exits and assemble at a safe point until cleared. If a power outage hits and you expect it back soon (some venues have generators that kick in), use battery-powered megaphones or simply loud voices to inform everyone of the situation and maybe take an early break. Safety first, always. Also, in pandemic-aware times, be prepared for health-related contingencies: have masks and sanitizers available, know how to handle if someone falls ill on-site (is there a first aid or isolation room?). Most venues have first aid personnel – know how to contact them fast. It’s beneficial to have a basic crisis plan documented, however brief, that covers these scenarios and roles (who speaks to media if needed, who liaises with venue security, etc.). It’s rare to need it, but invaluable if something big occurs. Attendee Issues: This ranges from minor (lost belongings) to serious (code of conduct violations or medical emergencies). For lost items, have a plan for a lost-and-found at the info desk. For complaints or incidents (e.g., an attendee reports harassment or an uncomfortable situation), handle with discretion and importance. Designate a senior committee member as the contact for such issues and make sure attendees quietly know who to talk to (some conferences include a “If you encounter any issue, please contact our help desk or so-and-so at this number” message in the program). Follow your code of conduct procedures: that might involve warning or expelling an offender if behavior crosses the line – hopefully never needed, but you must be prepared to enforce a safe environment. Medical emergencies should be handled by professionals: call emergency services if needed; venues often have a protocol for summoning medical aid. Know the location of the nearest hospital and keep a basic first aid kit on hand for minor injuries. Throughout any crisis, communication is your best tool . Keep attendees informed in a calm, concise manner. Utilize multiple channels: live announcements, push notifications on the app, and notices on info boards. People are surprisingly understanding when kept in the loop. It’s when they’re left wondering that frustration mounts. Also, lean on your team – you as an organizer don’t have to solve everything personally. Delegate tasks to the capable people you’ve assembled and trust them to carry it out. After any significant incident, debrief with the team to learn from it. Many seasoned organisers say some of their best improvements came from lessons learned “the hard way” when something went wrong. Orchestrating Your On-Site Operations — How real-time communication keeps your team synchronized during peak hours Closing and Follow-Up As the conference winds down, plan a satisfying closing session or at least a moment of closure. This could be a final keynote, a panel reflecting on next steps in the field, or even a fun wrap-up (some events do award ceremonies or a video montage of highlights). Thank everyone – attendees, speakers, sponsors, volunteers – for their contributions. Announce any upcoming related events or the next edition of the conference if it’s recurring. A strong closing can leave attendees with a positive final impression, which is what they carry home. Immediately after the conference, while details are fresh, document what went well and what didn’t. Collect staff feedback and any notable comments from attendees that you heard in person. Sending the post-event survey within a day or two is ideal – keep it short, but ask key questions (e.g., rate the venue, rate the content, what was most valuable, suggestions for improvement). Analyzing this feedback will provide evidence of success (e.g., “95% of respondents were satisfied with the conference format”) that can be used in sponsor reports or future promotions, as well as point out areas to work on. For example, maybe many people wanted parallel sessions recorded – that could justify AV budget next time for recording equipment. Don’t forget to fulfill any post-conference deliverables . This might include sending certificates of attendance or presentation (some academics need these for their institution records or continuing education credits). If you promised proceedings or journal special issue publications of selected papers, coordinate with publishers to make sure authors submit final versions on time, and get those published – often proceedings are released a few months after the event. Upload slides or poster PDFs to the event website if you plan to share those (make sure you have presenter consent). And tie up loose ends with finances: pay any remaining venue or vendor bills, reconcile the budget, and ensure sponsors get what they paid for (e.g., maybe a mailing list of opt-in attendees, if that was part of the deal). Lastly, celebrate with your team. Running an academic conference is a substantial achievement – it’s often said that it’s like “herding cats” because academics are very independent-minded and details can be arduous. Take a moment to acknowledge your committee and volunteers, perhaps in a post-event get-together or at least a thank-you letter. Not only is this well-deserved, but it also helps in retaining enthusiastic organizers for the future. Many conferences build a legacy by rotating some of the committee while keeping a core of experienced planners who carry knowledge forward year to year. By recognizing everyone’s efforts and capturing the wisdom gained, you ensure that the next conference – whether next year or next decade – will be even better. Frequently Asked Questions How long does it take to plan an academic conference? Planning an academic conference typically requires 12 to 18 months for large international events and six to nine months for smaller symposia. Organizers should establish a master timeline early, starting with defining objectives, forming a committee, and securing a venue before announcing the call for papers. What is a Call for Papers (CFP) in academic conferences? A Call for Papers is an official announcement inviting researchers to submit their work for conference presentation. It outlines the event’s theme, accepted submission types like full papers or extended abstracts, formatting guidelines, and critical deadlines. Organizers usually release the CFP nine to twelve months before the event. How does the peer review process work for academic conferences? The peer review process involves evaluating submitted abstracts or papers through a program committee of subject matter experts. Conferences typically use a double-blind review model where two to four reviewers assess each submission over four to six weeks based on originality, methodology, and significance before final selection. How should you allocate the budget for an academic conference? A standard academic conference budget allocates approximately 40% to venue and catering, 20% to audio-visual equipment, and 15% to social events. Event planners should also include a 10% contingency fund to cover unexpected last-minute expenses while estimating revenue from registration fees, institutional support, and sponsorships. What are the different session formats at an academic conference? Academic conferences feature diverse session formats including 30-to-60-minute plenary keynotes, 15-to-20-minute oral paper presentations, and 45-to-60-minute panel discussions. Events also incorporate interactive elements like two-to-three-hour skill-building workshops, one-to-two-hour poster sessions, and structured networking events to maximize attendee engagement and knowledge sharing. Why is early-bird pricing important for conference registration? Early-bird pricing incentivizes attendees to register months in advance by offering discounted ticket rates. This strategy provides organizers with crucial upfront funding to cover early expenses like venue deposits, helps gauge overall event interest, and reduces last-minute administrative bottlenecks closer to the conference date. What audio-visual equipment is required for an academic conference? Essential audio-visual equipment for academic sessions includes a projector or large display, presenter laptop connections, a laser pointer, and at least one microphone. Larger halls require comprehensive sound systems with multiple microphones for audience Q&A, while hybrid events need reliable internet bandwidth supporting two to three devices per attendee. How do you organize a successful academic poster session? Organizing a successful poster session requires scheduling it as an exclusive activity, typically during a late afternoon reception between 5:00 PM and 7:00 PM. Organizers should group posters by theme, provide clear dimensional guidelines, supply mounting materials, and incorporate engaging elements like one-minute lightning previews or poster competitions. How can conference organizers improve attendee networking? Organizers can enhance networking by launching pre-conference online discussion boards and hosting first-timer orientations on opening day. Incorporating interactive formats like roundtable discussions, gamified digital scavenger hunts, and informal Meet the Professor sessions helps break the ice and fosters meaningful collaborations among researchers at all career stages. What should you do if a conference speaker cancels last minute? If a speaker cancels unexpectedly, organizers should avoid leaving an empty schedule slot. Effective contingency plans include having the session chair lead an open audience discussion on the topic, extending the Q&A period for previous speakers, or utilizing a standby presentation from a local backup researcher. What happens after an academic conference concludes? After a conference concludes, organizers must send post-event surveys to gather attendee feedback and measure success metrics. Post-conference duties also include distributing attendance certificates, publishing selected papers in proceedings or journal special issues, reconciling the final budget, and sharing event analytics with sponsors to secure future partnerships.

title: From request to resolution: How Front AI runs the work, not just the reply

body_text: Replies are easy. Getting the work done isn’t. Megan Beatty, Head of Product at Front, breaks down how Front’s latest AI updates move work from request to resolution. Most AI in customer operations was built for the easy stuff. Password resets. Order lookups. Anything a help center article can handle. For that kind of work, it’s fine. But the requests that actually stress out operations teams aren’t simple. They span systems, handoffs, and judgment calls that depend on context nobody paused to document. That’s where most AI stops — and where your team picks up the slack. 24% of teams said their existing AI tools were actually creating more coordination work, not less. That’s not just a tool problem. It’s a design problem. Most AI was never built to handle what you actually deal with. We’ve spent a decade building for that complexity. Today, we’re shipping three updates to Front AI that work from a different assumption: the job doesn’t end at the reply. Autopilot Playbooks automate your complex business processes Autopilot Resolve lets customers complete requests from start to finish right in your app or website Copilot is now your team’s AI assistant to figure out next steps, find information, and solve problems Make the work run itself with Autopilot Playbooks Prior to working on AI at Front, our Head of AI Kevin Yang ran EAT Club, a food delivery company. Every day, his team would get flooded with “Where’s my order?” questions at lunchtime. Sounds like a simple enough question. But it’s actually a multi-step, multi-system, multi-team workflow to solve: checking the order system, the restaurant, the driver’s location, then deciding what to do next — wait for it to arrive, refund the customer, or give them the option to order something new. And all of that had to happen thousands of times, within a 60-minute window. This is exactly the kind of complex work Autopilot Playbooks are built for. With Playbooks, you can: Let AI take on the work that slows your team down, from multi-step requests to cross-system actions Automate with control, using guardrails and handoffs when human judgment is needed Handle edge cases without mapping them all, so the process keeps running as things change The shift is simple but important: Instead of relying on people to coordinate the work, the work coordinates itself. That means fewer handoffs, clearer ownership, and processes that hold up even when things get messy or volume spikes. And you don’t have to map every possible edge case up front. If you have a process for it, Playbooks can run it. “Autopilot Playbooks proactively capture the key information we need from customers, automating a lot of the time-consuming back-and-forth between systems. Playbooks helped reduce the time spent on scheduling by 90%, freeing up our customer service representatives to focus on solving customers’ problems.” Dan Fritsch Director of Operations at Central Storage & Warehouse Don’t deflect. Resolve. With live chat, customers don’t want faster replies — they want the job done. Most AI agents handle the easy stuff: password resets, quick lookups. The complex requests, coordination across teams, multi-step troubleshooting, land back on your team. They send a "let me check on that," but customers aren’t getting solutions sooner. For requests that can’t be fully handled in the moment, Resolve creates a ticket with full context. Resolve would run the Playbook to confirm the order, check status across systems, and move straight to the right outcome, whether that’s an update, a replacement, or a refund, without waiting for someone on your team to pick it up. And if something did need a human, it would arrive with all the context already in place. Instead of just deflecting, Resolve executes. It carries context through every step, so requests don’t stall out or restart as they move between systems or teams. “Front is a key partner in Ridepanda’s AI strategy. We’re focused on deploying Autopilot in the areas where it delivers the most value, automating the right conversations while preserving high-touch work for our team. This allows us to reduce coordination overhead and drive better outcomes.” Cassidy Grace Senior CX Manager at Ridepanda Copilot helps teams handle the unpredictable Good responses require full context — the account history, the open threads, the last three handoffs. As Head of Product, I get pulled into customer calls all the time, often with very little notice. Getting ready for a meeting means digging around in Salesforce, call notes, and past conversations to get up to speed on an account. Now, I just start with Copilot. Copilot turns the signals scattered across your customer conversations into something you can actually act on. It pulls together everything it knows about the account from threads and connected tools like Gong and Salesforce. In just a few minutes, Copilot creates a clear picture of the relationship and what’s likely to come up in the conversation. The entire flow, from research to meeting prep, goes from hours to just 15 minutes. With Copilot, you can: Find how similar issues were handled before by searching conversations across teams and inboxes, so you don’t have to track them down yourself Get answers from threads, knowledge, and connected systems like CRM and billing, without jumping between tools Understand what’s going on with a customer or account across teams like sales, support, and finance before you respond The result shows up in the moments that matter. Copilot pulls all of it together before your team hits reply, so they spend their time on the judgment call, not the detective work. Get started with Autopilot and Copilot, built for real, complex customer work This is everything we’ve been building toward at Front: not just faster replies, but systems that actually complete the work — especially for customers with high-stakes, complex operations where AI hasn’t been able to deliver. Autopilot executes the routine processes through Playbooks. Resolve lets your customers get instant resolutions in real time, or a seamless handoff to your team. And Copilot supports your team in the moments that still require human judgment, bringing them up to speed to make the right call. Together, they’re built for customer operations where the work is messy, the stakes are high, and the job doesn’t stop at the reply.
